name: Bilal Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Bilal, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the primary crusher at a copper and gold mine. The haul trucks tip their rock into a huge steel bin, and my crusher breaks boulders the size of a car down to the size of a football, then it all goes off on the conveyors to the mill. I'm the senior operator on my roster, so I sit in the crusher control room watching the screens, and I go out and walk the belts and the chutes when something sounds wrong. I like solving problems, like a chute blocking or the crusher choking on wet clay. What wears me out is the noise and the twelve-hour nights, and being paid as an operator when half the time I'm doing an engineer's thinking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Give me an example of that engineer's thinking.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The crusher has steel liners that wear out, and changing them means a two-day shutdown. Last year I used an AI tool to build a spreadsheet from five years of wear readings, and it predicted the change three weeks better than the old schedule. I showed the maintenance boss my liner spreadsheet, and he took it to head office with his name on it, which tells you something about who gets the credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a pity, because the tools are useful if you know how to use them. At work I'd keep telling people to try them. Online I'd say people got carried away, both the ones who were scared and the ones who were selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed. I've been hoping AI would make my kind of thinking count for more. But for my pay packet and my mortgage, nothing changes, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the tools every day, keep improving the liner spreadsheet, and maybe offer it to the other mines in the group. I'd try to save a bit, though with the mortgage it's hard. Mostly I'd carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little disappointment in there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is money so tight for someone at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We bought our house late, at forty-nine, because we'd rented for years. So the mortgage runs to my seventies on paper. Then our son started his electrical apprenticeship and we bought his tools, which wasn't cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'my kind of thinking counting for more' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being paid for the problem-solving, not just the hours in the chair. I'm the cheapest engineer this mine has, because on paper I'm just the man watching the crusher.

S0.say: It's a pity, because the tools are useful if you know how to use them; people got carried away, both the scared ones and the sellers. He'd keep telling colleagues to try them.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I hoped AI would make my kind of thinking count for more. For my pay and mortgage, nothing changes, which is fine.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools daily, improves the liner spreadsheet and offers it to other mines in the group. Tries to save a little despite the mortgage and otherwise carries on.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of disappointment.
S0.quote: I'm the cheapest engineer this mine has, because on paper I'm just the man watching the crusher.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal is an inventive operator who already uses AI to do engineering-level work and resents not being paid or credited for it. A plateau mildly disappoints him. His thin savings come from buying a house late and paying for his son's apprenticeship tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but say it kindly. I'd tell people the company and the government both owe us decent training, and we owe it to ourselves to take it. I'd post the courses I find in our crew's group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The crusher can mostly run itself already, so it's not the operating that keeps me in a job, it's the fixing and the knowing. If AI takes the routine bits, people like me become the ones who keep the whole system running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be trained as an automation technician, the person who maintains the sensors and control systems, and I'd do online courses at night with AI as my tutor. I'd bring my liner tool to the planning meetings and ask for a proper role building more of them. I'd ask for a pay grade to match, and if they said no, I'd start looking at the other mine down the coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. It's the first time in years I'd feel like the wind was behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's another mine down the coast. Isn't moving hard at your age, with few jobs around?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three hours away, so it'd be a fly-in, drive-out roster, two weeks there and one home. Claire wouldn't love it. But the jobs that'd be growing are the technical ones, and they'd be looking for people who know crushers and computers both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger operators who only know how to watch screens, oddly enough. Everyone thinks the old guys are in trouble. I think the kid who only knows the screen is in more trouble than the old guy who knows the machine.

S1.say: Adapt or get left behind, but say it kindly: the company and government owe us training, and we owe it to ourselves to take it. He'd share the courses he finds in his crew's group chat.
S1.think: It's good for me, because the crusher can mostly run itself already and it's the fixing and knowing that keep me employed. People like me become the ones who keep the whole system running.
S1.do: Asks to train as an automation technician and studies online at night with AI as a tutor. Brings his liner tool to planning meetings, asks for a matching pay grade, and looks at the other mine down the coast if refused.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the wind is finally behind him.
S1.quote: Everyone thinks the old guys are in trouble. I think the kid who only knows the screen is in more trouble than the old guy who knows the machine.
S1.fieldNote: Bilal sees steady change as his chance to be recognised for skills he already has. He would bargain for pay and walk if refused, despite his age and few local options. His view that screen-only young operators are more exposed than older machine experts was unexpected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan from government and business together, because this is bigger than any one company. And I'd say people should learn what they can, but nobody should be blamed for not keeping up with something this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, in two years even my job goes. If the AI can diagnose the crusher better than me and a robot can change the liners, there's no technician role to grow into. I'd be sixty with a mortgage until my seventies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to sell what I know while it's still worth something, maybe contract work setting up AI maintenance systems at smaller mines that are behind. I'd cut everything else and talk to the bank about stretching or pausing the mortgage. I'd use the AI to find every grant or scheme going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel I could do something, but the clock would be loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years change how you'd use your head start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, my head start is maybe twelve months, so I'd have to cash it in fast. Being early only matters if there's a race long enough to win. Two years is a sprint where the finish line keeps moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to the bank. What's the conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go in with a spreadsheet, of course. Here's what we owe, here's what we can pay, here's a plan. Claire says I'm the only man who'd bring a chart to his own foreclosure, but I'd rather that than wait for the letter.

S2.say: We need a proper plan from government and business together, because this is bigger than any one company. People should learn what they can, but nobody should be blamed for not keeping up with something this fast.
S2.think: In two years even my job goes, because AI could diagnose the crusher and a robot could change the liners. I'd be sixty with a mortgage running into my seventies.
S2.do: Sells his know-how as contract work setting up AI maintenance systems at smaller mines. Cuts everything else, takes a spreadsheet plan to the bank to stretch or pause the mortgage, and uses AI to find every grant or scheme.
S2.feel: Anxious, still able to act but with a loud clock.
S2.quote: Being early only matters if there's a race long enough to win. Two years is a sprint where the finish line keeps moving.
S2.fieldNote: Bilal's head start shrinks to about a year in the two-year picture, and he would cash it in fast with contract work. He stays practical rather than frozen, even planning the bank conversation with a spreadsheet. He doesn't blame workers or any single side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people start now. I'd tell my crew to learn the systems, and the company to train them on the clock. That's fair to both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. I could become the automation technician, then probably help install the robots that replace the rest of the plant, and be useful right to the end. That might even pay down the mortgage faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the automation course and get the ticket, and push for a formal technician role. I'd offer to help run the first robot liner changes, so I'm the one who knows them. Any pay rise would go on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mainly about the fact I'd be helping put people out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be helping install machines that replace your mates. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easily. But if I don't, someone from a city contractor will, and they won't care who they're replacing. If someone's going to switch off the lights on this crusher, I'd rather it was someone who knows everyone's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build a real role rather than just sell a trick. With two years I'd be grabbing money. With five, I'd be building something that lasts until I can retire.

S3.say: Five years is enough to prepare if people start now: crews should learn the systems and the company should train them on the clock. That's fair to both sides.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, and I could become the automation technician and help install the robots, staying useful to the end. That might even pay the mortgage down faster.
S3.do: Finishes the automation course in the first year and pushes for a formal technician role. Volunteers to help run the first robot liner changes and puts any pay rise on the mortgage.
S3.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly about helping put others out of work.
S3.quote: If someone's going to switch off the lights on this crusher, I'd rather it was someone who knows everyone's name.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Bilal build a lasting role rather than cash in a trick. His discomfort is moral: he would be helping replace his own crew. He reasons that it is better done by someone who knows everyone's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Get the training in place, keep the older ones on until their pensions, give the young ones new skills. Sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so I'd see most of it from inside, then retire. I'd have time to become the technician, maybe train others. It's probably the best of the five for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the slower one but without the rush. Year one I'd do the course and keep building my tools. I'd also start teaching a night class at the community college on AI for tradespeople, a bit of extra money and something I'd enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach a night class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm sick of watching good tradespeople think these tools aren't for them. My son's mates are electricians and plumbers and they use it like a toy. I'd teach plumbers to use AI like a spirit level, not like a fortune teller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years let you put anything aside at last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the technician pay comes through and the night class adds a bit, we could finally have three months saved by sixty. Claire would frame the bank statement.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so use it: get training in place, keep older workers on to their pensions and give the young new skills. Sensible stuff.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight, so I'd see most of it from inside and then retire. It's probably the best of the five for me.
S4.do: Does the automation course without rushing and keeps building his tools. Starts teaching a paid night class on AI for tradespeople at the community college.
S4.quote: I'd teach plumbers to use AI like a spirit level, not like a fortune teller.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Bilal is hopeful and even imagines finally having three months saved. His night class idea comes from frustration that tradespeople treat AI as a toy. He frames the decade as a gift that only counts if people use it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even being early doesn't help when it's that fast, and the mortgage doesn't care how clever you are. What would help is the banks being told to give mining families breathing room on mortgages, and a bridge to the pension for people over fifty-five.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about credit. Operators like me do the thinking and the boss gets the name on it. If the robots come, I'd at least like the record to show who taught them.

headlineQuote: I showed the maintenance boss my liner spreadsheet, and he took it to head office with his name on it, which tells you something about who gets the credit.
portrait: Bilal Dubois is a 58-year-old senior crusher operator at a copper and gold mine who already uses AI to do engineering-level work, like predicting liner wear, without the pay or credit for it. He bought his house late and paid for his son's apprenticeship tools, so the mortgage runs into his seventies and there is almost nothing saved. Pragmatic and in the middle politically, he sees steady change and the slower AGI scenarios as chances to become the technician who keeps the machines running. The two-year scenario makes him anxious because his head start shrinks to a year, but he stays practical rather than frozen.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even being early wouldn't help at that speed and his mortgage runs into his seventies.
whatWouldHelp: Banks giving mining families breathing room on mortgages and a bridge to the pension for workers over fifty-five.
